title: The numbers
summary: Every number a beginner needs to read a campaign, from impressions to profit, worked through one Example campaign from start to finish. You finish with break-even values for every metric and a daily sheet that turns raw counts into decisions.

lessons.title: Impressions, reach, frequency and CPM
objectives: By the end you can explain the difference between impressions and reach.
Calculate frequency and CPM from the numbers in an ads report.
Spot when rising frequency is a sign of ad fatigue.

steps.h: Numbers are how you see your money
steps.p: An ad account is a stream of numbers. Each one answers a simple question: how many people saw the ad, how many acted, what it cost and what came back. This module teaches every number a beginner needs, one at a time, using one Example campaign all the way through.

d.s: Seen? Clicked? Signed up? Paid back?

steps.say: Here's the big idea for this whole module. An ad account is really just a stream of numbers, and each one answers a simple question. Did people see the ad? Did they click? Did they sign up? Did they pay, and did it pay you back? We'll learn every number a beginner needs, one at a time, and we'll use one Example campaign all the way through, so you can watch each number connect to the next.

steps.p: Money moves through the same stages on almost every campaign. You pay for the ad to be shown. Some people click. Some of those sign up. Some of those pay. Each stage has its own number. This lesson covers the first stage: being seen.
steps.say: Look at the flow on screen. Money moves through the same stages on almost every campaign. You pay for the ad to be shown. Some people click. Some of those sign up. Some of those deposit, and then you get paid out. Each stage has its own number, and that's why this module is built in this order. This first lesson covers the very first stage, being seen.

steps.p: An impression is one showing of your ad on a screen. Reach is the number of different people who saw it at least once. If one person sees your ad three times, that counts as three impressions and a reach of one.
steps.more: Reach is an estimate. Platforms count people across phones, browsers and accounts using their own models, so treat reach as a close estimate. Each platform also has its own rule for when an impression counts, for example how much of the ad must appear on screen. Check the platform's help pages for the current definition; names and definitions change.
d: Impressions|every time the ad is shown
steps.say: Let's separate two words beginners mix up. An impression is one showing of your ad on a screen. Reach is the number of different people who saw it at least once. So if one person sees your ad three times, that's three impressions, but a reach of just one. Keep in mind that reach is an estimate, because platforms count people across phones, browsers and accounts using their own models. Definitions also change, so check the platform's help pages.

steps.p: Frequency tells you how many times, on average, each person saw your ad. Divide impressions by reach. A frequency of 1.6 means the average person saw the ad 1.6 times. In practice some saw it once and some saw it three or four times.
steps.say: Frequency tells you how many times, on average, each person saw your ad. The formula is right there: impressions divided by reach. A frequency of one point six means the average person saw the ad one point six times. Of course, nobody sees an ad point six times. In practice, some people saw it once, and some saw it three or four times. Frequency is the average across all of them.

steps.p: Example: our practice campaign has 16,000 impressions and a reach of 10,000 people. 16,000 divided by 10,000 is 1.6. We will use this same campaign through the whole module so you can see how every number connects to the next one.
steps.more: The Example campaign: $40 spent on one ad set, in one country, over one day. In the next lessons you will meet its clicks, sign-ups, deposits and payout. All of its figures are invented for teaching. They are not a forecast and not a promise of what you will see on your own campaigns.
steps.say: Now let's meet our practice campaign. Example: it has sixteen thousand impressions and a reach of ten thousand people. Sixteen thousand divided by ten thousand is one point six. That's our frequency. Behind it is forty dollars spent on one ad set, in one country, over one day. All of its figures are invented for teaching. They're not a forecast, and not a promise of what you'll see on your own campaigns.

steps.p: CPM means cost per mille, and mille is Latin for thousand. It is what you paid for 1,000 impressions. Think of it as the price of attention on a platform. It is the first cost you pay on almost every social media campaign.
steps.say: Next, C P M, cost per mille. Mille is Latin for thousand, so C P M is what you paid for one thousand impressions. Follow the formula on screen: spend, divided by impressions, times one thousand. Think of it as the price of attention on a platform. It's the first cost you pay on almost every social media campaign, so it's worth knowing well.

steps.p: Example: $40 spent for 16,000 impressions. $40 divided by 16,000 is $0.0025 per impression. Multiply by 1,000 and the CPM is $2.50. In plain words, every 1,000 showings of the ad cost $2.50.
steps.more: You can turn the formula around to plan a test: Impressions = Spend ÷ CPM × 1,000. If you plan to spend $40 and expect a CPM near $2.50, expect about 16,000 impressions ($40 ÷ $2.50 × 1,000). If you think an ad needs at least 10,000 impressions before you judge it, and CPM in your geo is near $4.00, you need about $40 ($4.00 × 10). All of these figures are Examples.
steps.say: Let's work it through. Example: forty dollars spent for sixteen thousand impressions. Forty divided by sixteen thousand is a quarter of a cent per impression. Multiply by one thousand, and the C P M is two dollars fifty. In plain words, every thousand showings of the ad cost two dollars fifty. You can also flip this around to plan a test, working out how many impressions a budget should buy. These figures are examples.

steps.h: What pushes CPM up or down
steps.p: CPM is set by an auction, so it moves with competition. More advertisers chasing the same people means higher prices. You met the auction in the Traffic 101 module. These are the common drivers to look at when your CPM changes from one week to the next.
steps.more: Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical: CPM in a high-income country is often several times higher than in many African markets for a similar audience. A cheap geo is still not automatically a better geo. Cheap attention from people who cannot or will not pay is expensive in the end. You will judge CPM using the later numbers in this module.
d: Audience|narrow or popular groups cost more
Placement|feeds, stories and reels price differently
Ad quality|low relevance can raise your price
steps.say: C P M is set by an auction, so it moves with competition. More advertisers chasing the same people means higher prices. Look at the cards for the common drivers: the geo, since richer markets usually cost more, the audience, the season, the placement, and your ad quality, because low relevance can raise your price. When your C P M changes from one week to the next, these are the first places to look.

steps.h: A cheap CPM is not a win by itself
steps.p: A low CPM only tells you that attention was cheap. If the people seeing your ad never click, never sign up or never deposit, those cheap impressions still lose money. Always read CPM together with what happens after the impression.

d.text: Judge CPM next to clicks, sign-ups and deposits, never alone.

steps.say: Here's a warning worth remembering. A low C P M only tells you that attention was cheap. If the people seeing your ad never click, never sign up and never deposit, those cheap impressions still lose money. Cheap attention from people who can't or won't pay ends up expensive. So always read C P M together with what happens after the impression, never on its own.

steps.p: When the same people see the same ad again and again, they stop noticing it. Frequency climbs and the click-through rate (the share who click, covered next lesson) slides down. This is called ad fatigue. Watching both lines together tells you when an ad is getting tired.
steps.more: There is no single frequency number at which every ad dies. A strong ad shown to a big audience can run at a high frequency for weeks. A weak ad shown to a small audience can tire in days. Use your own data: when frequency rises and results per dollar fall at the same time, prepare a new creative or widen the audience.
steps.say: Look at the two lines on this chart. As the same people see the same ad again and again, they stop noticing it. Frequency climbs, and the click-through rate, the share who click, slides down. That's called ad fatigue. These figures are an example, and there's no single frequency number where every ad dies. Use your own data: when frequency rises and results per dollar fall together, prepare a new creative or widen the audience.

steps.p: Before you move on, practise reading these four numbers on any campaign report you can see, even an old one or a sample from a colleague. Speed comes from repetition, and you will use these every single day.
steps.more: If your own CPM differs slightly from the platform's, it is usually rounding. A large difference usually means you picked a different date range, a different level (campaign, ad set or ad) or the wrong column.
d: Compare with the platform's own figure
steps.say: Before you move on, practise reading these four numbers on any report you can see, even an old one or a sample from a colleague. Follow the checklist. Find spend and impressions. Work out C P M yourself. Divide impressions by reach. Then compare with the platform's own figure. A small difference is usually rounding. A big one usually means a different date range, a different level, or the wrong column.

steps.h: Common mistakes with the first four numbers
steps.p: These slips look small, and each one quietly changes a decision about real money. They are worth learning now, while the numbers are still simple and you only have four of them to watch.
d: Reading reach as impressions|reach counts people, not showings
Comparing different date ranges|same dates, same level
Judging CPM alone|follow it to cost per result
Ignoring frequency|watch it next to CTR for fatigue
Rounding too early|keep decimals in your sheet
steps.say: Finally, the common mistakes. Reading reach as impressions, when reach counts people, not showings. Comparing different date ranges, instead of the same dates at the same level. Judging C P M alone, instead of following it to cost per result. Ignoring frequency, when you should watch it next to click-through rate for fatigue. And rounding too early, so keep the decimals in your sheet. Each slip quietly changes a decision about real money.

takeaways: Impressions count showings, reach counts people, and frequency is impressions ÷ reach.
CPM is spend ÷ impressions × 1,000: the price of 1,000 showings.
Rising frequency with a falling CTR is a common sign of ad fatigue.

glossary.def: One showing of an ad on a screen. One person can create many impressions.
The estimated number of different people who saw an ad at least once.
Impressions divided by reach: the average number of times each person saw the ad.
Cost per mille (thousand): spend divided by impressions, times 1,000.
When an audience has seen an ad so often that fewer people respond to it.

quiz.q: An ad got 9,000 impressions and reached 3,000 people. What is the frequency?
quiz.why: Frequency is impressions ÷ reach, so 9,000 ÷ 3,000 = 3. The other answers subtract, flip or multiply the numbers.

quiz.q: You spent $30 and got 12,000 impressions. What is the CPM?
quiz.why: CPM = $30 ÷ 12,000 × 1,000 = $2.50. $0.0025 is the cost of a single impression, before multiplying by 1,000.

quiz.q: What does reach measure?
options: Different people who saw the ad at least once
Total times the ad was shown
quiz.why: Reach counts people, not showings. Total showings are impressions, and the cost of 1,000 showings is CPM.

quiz.q: Over a week, frequency rises from 1.2 to 3.4 while CTR falls by half. What is the most likely cause?
options: Ad fatigue: the same people keep seeing the same ad
quiz.why: Frequency climbing while CTR falls is the classic pattern of ad fatigue. Fast reach growth would push frequency down, not up.

quiz.q: Geo A has a $1.50 CPM and Geo B a $6.00 CPM. What can you conclude?
options: Geo A will be more profitable
Attention costs less in Geo A; profit depends on what happens after the impression
quiz.why: CPM only prices attention. Whether a geo makes money depends on clicks, sign-ups, deposits and payout, covered in the next lessons.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn the first four numbers in any ads report: impressions, reach, frequency and C P M. They tell you how many people saw your ad, how often, and what that attention cost, and every later number is built on top of them.
lessons.say_outro: So, impressions count showings, reach counts people, frequency is the average between them, and C P M is the price of a thousand showings. Your task: open any campaign report, yours or a sample, work out C P M and frequency by hand for the last seven days, and explain any difference from the platform's figures. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Clicks, CTR and CPC
objectives: By the end you can tell link clicks apart from all clicks.
Calculate CTR and CPC, and find CPC from CPM and CTR.
Explain why a high CTR on its own is not proof of a good ad.

steps.p: After someone sees your ad, the next thing you want is a click. A click means the ad made them curious enough to leave what they were doing. It is a small yes, and it is the first sign your message is working on real people.

d.b: A click is a small yes
d.s: Curious enough to leave the feed

steps.say: After someone sees your ad, the next thing you want is a click. A click means the ad made them curious enough to leave what they were doing in the feed. It's a small yes. And it matters, because it's the first sign that your message is actually working on real people, not just being shown to them.

steps.p: Platforms count several kinds of clicks. All clicks includes likes, comments, profile taps and taps to expand the text. Link clicks are only the taps that try to open your page or app. For funnel maths, use link clicks.
steps.more: Some platforms also report outbound clicks, unique clicks or landing page views. Names change; check the current Ads Manager. Whichever click metric you choose, use the same one every day so your numbers stay comparable from one day and one campaign to the next.

b.title: Link clicks
items: Start the trip to your page

steps.say: Look at the two columns. Platforms count several kinds of clicks. All clicks includes likes, reactions, profile taps, and taps on See more. Link clicks are only the taps that try to open your page or app. For funnel maths, use link clicks, because those are the people starting the trip to your offer. Names vary by platform and change, so whichever click metric you choose, use the same one every day.

steps.p: CTR means click-through rate. It is the share of impressions that turned into a click. It tells you how well the whole ad, meaning the image or video, the words and the offer together, earns a reaction from the people who see it.
steps.say: C T R means click-through rate. It's the share of impressions that turned into a click. The formula's on screen: link clicks, divided by impressions, times one hundred. It tells you how well the whole ad, meaning the image or video, the words and the offer together, earns a reaction from the people who see it.

steps.p: Example: the practice campaign from the last lesson had 16,000 impressions and got 240 link clicks. 240 divided by 16,000 is 0.015. Multiply by 100 and the CTR is 1.5%. Out of every 1,000 showings, 15 people clicked.
steps.say: Back to our practice campaign. Example: sixteen thousand impressions and two hundred and forty link clicks. Two hundred and forty divided by sixteen thousand is zero point zero one five. Times one hundred, that's a C T R of one point five percent. Put simply, out of every thousand showings, fifteen people clicked.

steps.p: CPC means cost per click. It is what you paid, on average, for each click. Even when the platform charges you by impression, you can still work out what each click cost by dividing your spend by your link clicks.
steps.say: C P C means cost per click. It's what you paid, on average, for each click. Here's a useful point. Even when the platform charges you by impression, you can still work out what each click cost. Just divide your spend by your link clicks, as the formula shows.

steps.p: Example: $40 spent, 240 link clicks. $40 divided by 240 is $0.1667, which rounds to $0.17. Keep the extra decimals in your sheet and round only when you show the number, or small rounding errors pile up later.
steps.say: Example: forty dollars spent and two hundred and forty link clicks. Forty divided by two hundred and forty is about seventeen cents, zero point one six six seven before rounding. Here's a good habit. Keep the extra decimals in your sheet, and round only when you show the number. Otherwise small rounding errors pile up later as you build more numbers on top of this one.

steps.h: How CPM and CTR set your CPC
steps.p: On a campaign charged by impression, your CPC comes from two other numbers. Divide CPM by CTR times 1,000. Example: $2.50 ÷ (1.5% × 1,000) = $2.50 ÷ 15 = $0.1667. That is the same answer as before, found a different way.
steps.more: Why this matters: you control CTR far more than CPM. CPM is mostly set by the auction. CTR is mostly set by your creative and your targeting. If CTR doubles while CPM stays the same, CPC halves. That is why better creative is often the cheapest way to cut your costs.
steps.say: Now see how the numbers link up. On a campaign charged by impression, your C P C comes from C P M and C T R. Divide C P M by C T R times one thousand. Example: two dollars fifty, divided by fifteen, gives the same seventeen cents as before. Here's why it matters. C P M is mostly set by the auction, but C T R is mostly set by your creative and targeting. If C T R doubles and C P M stays the same, C P C halves.

steps.p: Example: two ads run in the same audience at the same $2.50 CPM. Ad A gets a 1% CTR, so each click costs $2.50 ÷ 10 = $0.25. Ad B gets a 2.5% CTR, so each click costs $2.50 ÷ 25 = $0.10. The better ad buys clicks for less than half the price.
steps.say: Look at these two bars. Example: two ads in the same audience, both at a two dollar fifty C P M. Ad A gets a one percent C T R, so each click costs twenty five cents. Ad B gets a two point five percent C T R, so each click costs just ten cents. Same price of attention, but the better ad buys clicks for less than half the price. That's the power of creative.

steps.p: A click does not mean the page loaded. Some people tap by accident, lose signal or close a slow page. Platforms often report landing page views: people whose page actually loaded. A big gap between clicks and page views is usually a speed or link problem.
steps.more: Example: 240 link clicks and 192 landing page views means 80% of clicks loaded the page (192 ÷ 240 = 0.8). The other 48 clicks were paid for and never saw your offer. The Funnels module covers how to make pages faster. Counting landing page views needs a pixel or similar tracking on your page; the Tracking basics module explains it (full setup: Tracking setup lab module).

Look at the funnel. Example: two hundred and forty clicks, but one hundred and ninety two page views, so eighty percent loaded. The other forty eight clicks were paid for and never saw your offer. steps.h: A high CTR is not the goal
steps.p: A shocking or vague ad can get a high CTR from curious people who never sign up. You pay for every one of those clicks. The real goal is clicks from people who want what the offer gives. Judge CTR together with what happens after the click.
steps.say: Here's a trap. A shocking or vague ad can get a high C T R from curious people who never sign up, and you pay for every one of those clicks. Compare the two columns. The clickbait ad has a high C T R but few sign-ups, and it can break ad policies. The honest ad may have a similar or lower C T R, but it brings more sign-ups per click and is safer for the account. Judge C T R together with what happens after the click.

steps.p: Example: an ad with 200 impressions and 3 clicks has a 1.5% CTR. One more click makes it 4 ÷ 200 = 2%. A single person moved the number by a third. Wait for enough impressions before you call an ad good or bad.
steps.more: Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical: many buyers wait for a few thousand impressions before reading CTR, and for more before reading anything further down the funnel. The fewer events behind a rate, the more it jumps around by chance. School 2 covers test size in depth.
steps.say: Small numbers lie. Example: an ad with two hundred impressions and three clicks has a one point five percent C T R. One more click makes it two percent. A single person moved the number by a third. So wait for enough impressions before you call an ad good or bad. As a rough guide, many buyers wait for a few thousand impressions before reading C T R, and that varies by geo and vertical.

steps.h: The formulas, ready for a sheet
steps.p: Type raw counts into a sheet and let formulas do the maths. Here, B is spend, C impressions, D link clicks and E landing page views, all in row 2. Copy the formulas down for every new day.

d.text:
CTR        =D2/C2        (format as %)
CPC        =B2/D2
CPC check  =(B2/C2*1000)/(D2/C2*1000)
Load rate  =E2/D2        (format as %)
d.note: Example layout. The CPC check is CPM ÷ (CTR × 1,000) and should match CPC.

steps.h: Before you judge an ad by its clicks
steps.p: Use this short list every time you look at CTR or CPC, so one lucky or unlucky day does not push you into a bad decision with real money.
d: Use link clicks, not all clicks
steps.say: Use this short checklist every time you look at C T R or C P C. Use link clicks, not all clicks. Wait for enough impressions. Compare C T R with sign-ups. And check clicks against page views. It takes a moment, and it stops one lucky or unlucky day from pushing you into a bad decision with real money.

steps.h: Common click mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: Clicks are the first number that feels like progress, which is why they mislead so often. Each mistake below makes an ad look better or worse than it is.
d: Calling a winner at 200 impressions|wait for a few thousand
Clickbait for CTR|judge CTR with sign-ups
Ignoring the click-to-page gap|check speed and the link
Mixing click metrics|pick one and keep it
steps.say: Clicks are the first number that feels like progress, which is why they mislead so often. Look at the cards. Using all clicks, when you should use link clicks. Calling a winner at two hundred impressions, instead of waiting for a few thousand. Chasing C T R with clickbait, instead of judging it with sign-ups. Ignoring the gap between clicks and page views. And mixing click metrics, instead of picking one and keeping it.

takeaways: Use link clicks for funnel maths. CTR = link clicks ÷ impressions × 100.
CPC = spend ÷ clicks, and also CPM ÷ (CTR × 1,000). Better creative lowers CPC.
A high CTR only matters if those clickers go on to sign up and pay.

quiz.q: CPM is $4.00 and CTR is 2%. What is the CPC?
Same spend on both. Ad X: 3% CTR, 300 clicks, 2 sign-ups. Ad Y: 1.2% CTR, 120 clicks, 12 sign-ups. Which ad did better?
options: Ad X, because its CTR is higher
You cannot compare ads with different CTRs

options: Page speed and whether the link works
quiz.why: A 40% gap between clicks and page views points to a slow page, a broken link or a redirect problem. The other numbers do not explain pages failing to load.

lessons.title: Conversion rate, CPL and CPA
objectives: By the end you can name the conversion your offer pays for.
Calculate CR, CPL and CPA (including cost per FTD).
Set a target CPA before you launch and explain why small samples mislead.

steps.p: Clicks cost money but do not pay you. You get paid when someone takes the action the offer pays for: a lead, a registration, a join or a first-time deposit. That action is called a conversion. This lesson teaches how to measure it and price it.

d.s: Know which action your offer pays for

steps.say: Here's a line worth remembering: conversions pay, clicks cost. Clicks cost money but don't pay you. You get paid when someone takes the action the offer pays for. That could be a lead, a registration, a join, or a first-time deposit. That action is called a conversion. In this lesson we'll measure it, and then we'll put a price on it.

steps.p: Different offers pay for different actions. Read your offer page to know exactly which one counts. A campaign can track several actions, but usually only one decides whether you get paid, so that is the one you price.
steps.more: FTD means first-time deposit: the first time a new user puts money into their account with the brand. Trading and gambling offers often pay on FTD, sometimes only if the deposit meets a minimum amount (a qualified FTD). These verticals are regulated: ads usually need platform authorization and must follow local law. Check both before running.
d: Registration|account created on the brand's site
FTD|first-time deposit, common in trading and iGaming
steps.say: Different offers pay for different actions, so look at the cards. A lead, where someone submits a name, phone or email. A registration on the brand's site. A join to your Telegram channel. An F T D, first-time deposit, common in trading and iGaming. And an install. Read your offer page to know exactly which one counts. Trading and gambling are regulated, so ads usually need platform authorization and must follow local law. Check both before running.

steps.p: Conversion rate, or CR, is the share of clicks that became conversions. Some buyers divide by landing page views instead of clicks. Either works, but choose one and use it every time, or your numbers will not compare across days or campaigns.
steps.say: Conversion rate, or C R, is the share of clicks that became conversions. The formula's on screen: conversions, divided by clicks, times one hundred. Some buyers divide by landing page views instead of clicks. Either works. But choose one and use it every time, or your numbers won't compare across days or campaigns.

steps.p: Example: the practice campaign's 240 clicks produced 36 sign-ups on the landing page. 36 divided by 240 is 0.15, so the click-to-lead CR is 15%. Fifteen of every 100 people who clicked left their details.
steps.say: Example: our practice campaign's two hundred and forty clicks produced thirty six sign-ups on the landing page. Thirty six divided by two hundred and forty is zero point one five, so the click-to-lead C R is fifteen percent. In plain words, fifteen of every hundred people who clicked left their details.

steps.p: CPL is what each lead cost you. Divide spend by the number of leads. A lead is someone who gave contact details or signed up but has not paid yet. CPL is useful early in a test, because leads arrive faster and in bigger numbers than deposits.
steps.say: C P L means cost per lead. Divide spend by the number of leads. A lead is someone who gave contact details or signed up, but hasn't paid yet. Here's why C P L is so useful early in a test. Leads arrive faster and in bigger numbers than deposits, so you get a readable signal sooner.

steps.p: Example: the practice campaign spent $40 and got 36 leads. $40 divided by 36 is $1.111, so the CPL is $1.11. Each person who signed up cost a little over one dollar in ad spend.
steps.say: Example: forty dollars spent, thirty six leads. Forty divided by thirty six is about one dollar eleven. So each person who signed up cost a little over one dollar in ad spend. Hold on to that number, because we'll compare it with break-even in a later lesson.

steps.p: CPA means cost per action: what you paid for each conversion the offer pays on. When that action is a first-time deposit, buyers call it cost per FTD, or CPFTD. This is the number you compare with your payout to see whether you made money.
steps.say: C P A means cost per action, what you paid for each conversion the offer pays on. When that action is a first-time deposit, buyers call it cost per F T D, sometimes written C P F T D. Look at the formula: spend, divided by paid actions. This is the number you compare with your payout to see whether you made money.

steps.p: Example: of the 36 leads, 2 made a first deposit. $40 divided by 2 FTDs is $20 per FTD. The lead-to-FTD rate is 2 ÷ 36, about 5.6%. Lesson 4 compares that $20 with the payout to find the profit.
steps.say: Example: of the thirty six leads, two made a first deposit. Forty dollars divided by two F T Ds is twenty dollars per F T D. The lead-to-F T D rate is two out of thirty six, about five point six percent. Later in this module, we'll compare that twenty dollars with the payout to find the profit.

steps.p: Here is the practice campaign from top to bottom. Each step loses people, and every lost person was paid for at the top. Seeing the full funnel in one picture helps you find which step is losing the most.
steps.say: Here's the whole Example funnel, top to bottom. Sixteen thousand impressions. Two hundred and forty clicks. Thirty six leads. Two F T Ds. Notice how each step loses people, and every lost person was paid for at the top. Seeing the full funnel in one picture helps you spot which step is losing the most.

steps.h: How each rate sets your cost per FTD
steps.p: Cost per FTD is built from the steps before it. Divide CPC by the click-to-lead rate times the lead-to-FTD rate. Example: $0.1667 ÷ (0.15 × 0.0556) = $0.1667 ÷ 0.00833 = $20. Improve any one step and the final cost falls.
steps.more: This is one of the most useful ideas in the module. If the click-to-lead rate rises from 15% to 20% and nothing else changes, cost per FTD falls from $20 to $15. Check: $0.1667 ÷ (0.20 × 0.0556) = $0.1667 ÷ 0.0111 = $15. A better landing page can cut CPA as much as a cheaper click can.
steps.say: This idea is one of the most useful in the module. Cost per F T D is built from the steps before it. Divide C P C by the click-to-lead rate times the lead-to-F T D rate. In our Example, that gives twenty dollars. Now, if the click-to-lead rate rose from fifteen to twenty percent and nothing else changed, cost per F T D would fall to fifteen dollars. So a better landing page can cut C P A as much as a cheaper click.

steps.p: Example: 2 FTDs on $40 is a $20 CPA. If one more person deposits on the same spend, it becomes $40 ÷ 3 = $13.33. If the next $40 brings nothing, it becomes $80 ÷ 2 = $40. With so few conversions, one person changes everything.
steps.more: Treat a CPA built on one, two or three conversions as a rough signal. Look at the steps above it as well, such as CPL and click-to-lead rate, which have more events behind them and move less by chance. The next slides and the Budget and kill rules module give firm starting rules for when to stop, hold or scale.
steps.say: Look how hard small samples swing. Example: two F T Ds on forty dollars is a twenty dollar C P A. If one more person deposits on the same spend, it drops to thirteen dollars thirty three. If the next forty dollars brings nothing, it jumps to forty dollars. With so few conversions, one person changes everything. So treat a C P A built on one, two or three conversions as a rough signal, and look at the steps above it too.

steps.h: Set a target CPA before you launch
steps.p: Your payout is the most you can pay per conversion and still break even. Decide how much of it you want to keep, then subtract. Example: the offer pays $30 per FTD and you want to keep $9, so your target CPA is $21.
steps.more: Lesson 5 covers break-even fully. For now: a CPA above the payout loses money, a CPA equal to the payout earns nothing, and a CPA at or under your target leaves the margin you planned. Write the target down before you spend, so a bad day does not tempt you to move it.
steps.say: Set a target C P A before you launch. Your payout is the most you can pay per conversion and still break even. Decide how much of it you want to keep, then subtract, as the formula shows. Example: the offer pays thirty dollars per F T D and you want to keep nine dollars, so your target C P A is twenty one dollars. Write it down before you spend, so a bad day doesn't tempt you to move it.

steps.h: Try it: the most you can pay per lead
steps.p: An offer pays $30 per FTD and about 5% of your leads deposit. You want to keep 30% of the payout. Work out the most you can pay per lead and still hit that margin, then check your answer.
steps.more: Break-even per lead is $30 × 5% = $1.50. Keeping 30% leaves $1.50 × 0.7 = $1.05. The practice campaign paid $1.11 per lead, so at a 5% deposit rate it would miss a 30% margin even though it still makes some profit. Figures are an example.

d.task: Payout $30, 5% of leads deposit, 30% margin. Max cost per lead?

steps.say: Now it's your turn. An offer pays thirty dollars per F T D, and about five percent of your leads deposit. You want to keep thirty percent of the payout. Your job is to work out the most you can pay per lead and still hit that margin. Start from what one lead is worth, then take off your margin. Use the calculator on screen. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Example: payout $30, target $21. Kill an ad set at $42 spend with 0 FTDs. From $63 spend, kill it if CPA is above $30, the lower of $31.50 and break-even. Scale +20% at most every 48 hours at CPA $16.80 or less with 3+ confirmed FTDs.
steps.more: These are starting rules, the same ones taught in the Budget and kill rules module. They use the network's confirmed count, never the platform's. Notice the practice campaign: $40 spent, 2 FTDs, CPA $20. It is under the $42 and $63 lines, so the rules say hold, even though the CPA is under target. Two FTDs are not enough to scale on.

d.text: Target $21: kill at $42 with 0. From $63, kill above $30. Scale at ≤ $16.80 with 3+ FTDs.

steps.say: Your target becomes your rules. Example: payout thirty dollars, target twenty one. Kill an ad set at forty two dollars spend with zero F T Ds. From sixty three dollars spend, kill it if C P A is above thirty dollars. Scale by twenty percent at most every forty eight hours, at a C P A of sixteen dollars eighty or less, with three or more confirmed F T Ds. These are starting rules, and they always use the network's confirmed count. Our practice campaign, with only two F T Ds, is a hold.

steps.p: Ads Manager may report 3 conversions while the network reports 2. Platforms estimate and attribute conversions in their own way, and some users are not tracked at all. You get paid on the network's count, so use it to judge CPA. The Tracking basics module explains the differences.

d.text: Use the network's count to judge profit. Use the platform's count to guide its delivery.

steps.say: Ads Manager may report three conversions while the network reports two. Platforms estimate and attribute conversions in their own way, and some users aren't tracked at all. You get paid on the network's count, so use it to judge C P A. The tip on screen puts it simply: use the network's count to judge profit, and use the platform's count to guide its delivery.

And target C P A, twenty one dollars. Notice that the twenty dollar cost per F T D sits just under the twenty one dollar target, so on these Example numbers it meets the plan.

steps.h: Common conversion mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: These mistakes all make a campaign look more or less profitable than it is. Every one is fixed by deciding your definitions before launch and sticking to them.
d: Pricing the wrong action|price the one the offer pays on
Using platform conversions|judge with the network count
Trusting a CPA from 1 or 2 FTDs|read the steps above it too
Moving the target after a bad day|write it down before launch
Switching CR denominators|clicks or page views, not both
steps.say: Finally, the common conversion mistakes. Pricing the wrong action, instead of the one the offer pays on. Using platform conversions, instead of the network count. Trusting a C P A from one or two F T Ds, without reading the steps above it. Moving the target after a bad day, when you should write it down before launch. And switching C R denominators. Every one is fixed by deciding your definitions before launch and sticking to them.

takeaways: A conversion is the action the offer pays for. Know exactly which one it is.
CR = conversions ÷ clicks × 100. CPL = spend ÷ leads. CPA = spend ÷ paid actions.
Set a target CPA from your payout before launch, and distrust CPAs built on very few conversions.

glossary.def: The action you are measuring, usually the one the offer pays for.
Conversion rate: conversions divided by clicks (or page views), times 100.
Cost per lead: spend divided by leads.

First-time deposit: a new user's first payment into their account with the brand.

quiz.q: 200 clicks produced 30 registrations. What is the CR?
quiz.why: CR = 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%. 6.7% comes from dividing clicks by registrations the wrong way.

quiz.q: You spent $90 and got 4 FTDs. What is your cost per FTD?
quiz.why: Cost per FTD = $90 ÷ 4 = $22.50. $360 multiplies instead of dividing.

quiz.q: The payout is $40 per FTD and you want to keep $10 of it. What is your target CPA?
quiz.why: Target CPA = payout − margin = $40 − $10 = $30. $40 is break-even, which leaves you nothing.

quiz.q: CPC is $0.20, click-to-lead rate is 10% and lead-to-FTD rate is 10%. What is the cost per FTD?
quiz.why: Cost per FTD = $0.20 ÷ (0.10 × 0.10) = $0.20 ÷ 0.01 = $20. Put another way, 100 clicks cost $20 and bring 10 leads and 1 FTD.

quiz.q: Ads Manager shows 5 FTDs and the network shows 3. Which count should you use to calculate profit?
options: Ads Manager, because it updates faster
The network, because it pays you on its own count
quiz.why: You are paid on the network's confirmed count, so profit must be judged on it. Platform counts are estimates that guide delivery.

lessons.title: Revenue, EPC, ROI and ROAS
objectives: By the end you can calculate revenue, profit and EPC for a campaign.
Calculate ROI and ROAS and convert one into the other.
Include every cost, and handle revenue that arrives later on RevShare.

steps.p: So far you measured what things cost. Now you measure what you earned. Revenue is the money the network owes you. Profit is what is left after you subtract what you spent. These two numbers decide whether a campaign deserves more money.
steps.say: Now we count what came back. Revenue is the money the network owes you. Profit is what's left after you subtract what you spent. The line on screen says it clearly: profit decides. These two numbers decide whether a campaign deserves more money, so let's learn to work them out properly.

steps.p: On a CPA deal, revenue is simple: the number of paid conversions times the payout for each one. Example: the practice campaign got 2 FTDs and the offer pays $30 per FTD, so revenue is 2 × $30 = $60.
steps.say: On a C P A deal, a cost per action deal, revenue is simple. It's the number of paid conversions times the payout for each one. Follow the formula. Example: our practice campaign got two F T Ds, first-time deposits, and the offer pays thirty dollars per F T D. So revenue is two times thirty, which is sixty dollars.

steps.p: Profit is revenue minus spend. Example: $60 revenue minus $40 of ad spend leaves $20 profit. If spend is bigger than revenue, the result is negative, which is a loss. Write losses as negative numbers so your totals add up correctly.
steps.say: Profit is revenue minus spend. Example: sixty dollars of revenue, minus forty dollars of ad spend, leaves twenty dollars profit. If spend is bigger than revenue, the result is negative, and that's a loss. Here's a good habit: write losses as negative numbers in your sheet, so your totals add up correctly.

steps.p: EPC is how much each click earned you on average. Divide revenue by clicks. Example: $60 ÷ 240 clicks = $0.25 per click. Compare it with the CPC of $0.17. When EPC is higher than CPC, each click earns more than it costs.
steps.say: E P C means earnings per click. It's how much each click earned you, on average. Divide revenue by clicks. Example: sixty dollars divided by two hundred and forty clicks is twenty five cents per click. Now compare that with the C P C, cost per click, of seventeen cents. When E P C is higher than C P C, each click earns more than it costs.

steps.p: EPC lets you compare offers on the same traffic in one number. If one offer earns $0.25 per click and another earns $0.12 on the same traffic, the first pays more for the same clicks, whatever their payouts look like on paper.
steps.more: Networks often show an EPC on the offer page. That figure is an average across many affiliates, geos and traffic types, so treat it as a rough guide at best. Your own EPC, measured on your own traffic, is the one that counts for your decisions.
steps.say: Here's why E P C is so useful. It lets you compare offers on the same traffic in one number. If one offer earns twenty five cents per click and another earns twelve cents on the same traffic, the first pays more for the same clicks, whatever their payouts look like on paper. Networks often show an E P C on the offer page, but that's an average across many affiliates, so treat it as a rough guide. Your own E P C is the one that counts.

steps.p: Example offer list with the network's EPC column, and your own EPC from your sheet. The network figure is an average across many affiliates and traffic types. The highlighted row shows why you decide on your own number.

blocks.value: My EPC = my revenue ÷ my clicks, from my sheet. Network EPC is a rough guide only.

steps.say: Here's an Example offer list. It shows the network's E P C next to your own. Look at the highlighted row, the kitchen set. The network says thirty one cents, but your own E P C is only twelve cents. The accessories offer shows the opposite. The network figure is an average across many affiliates and traffic types, so this is why you decide on your own number, worked out from your revenue and your clicks.

steps.p: ROI tells you how much profit you made for every dollar you spent, as a percentage. Example: ($60 − $40) ÷ $40 × 100 = 50%. Every $1 spent came back as that same $1 plus $0.50 of profit.
steps.say: R O I means return on investment. It tells you how much profit you made for every dollar you spent, as a percentage. The formula: revenue minus spend, divided by spend, times one hundred. Example: sixty minus forty is twenty, divided by forty is a half, so fifty percent. In plain words, every dollar spent came back as that same dollar, plus fifty cents of profit.

steps.p: ROAS compares revenue with ad spend and leaves profit out of it. Example: $60 ÷ $40 = 1.5. It is often written as 1.5x or 150%. A ROAS of 1.0 means you only got your money back. Below 1.0 you lost money.
steps.say: R O A S means return on ad spend. It compares revenue with ad spend and leaves profit out of it. Example: sixty dollars divided by forty dollars is one point five. It's often written as one point five x, or one hundred and fifty percent. A R O A S of one point oh means you only got your money back. Below one point oh, you lost money.

steps.h: Try it: ROAS from spend and revenue
steps.p: Use the practice campaign: $40 of ad spend and $60 of confirmed revenue. Work out the ROAS, then check your answer. Afterwards, change the revenue to $40 and $30 and see where break-even sits.
steps.more: $60 ÷ $40 = 1.5. At $40 revenue ROAS is 1.0, break-even. At $30 it is 0.75, a 25% loss. ROI is ROAS minus 1, times 100: 50%, 0% and −25%.

d.task: Spend $40, revenue $60. What is the ROAS?

steps.say: Time to practise. Use the practice campaign: forty dollars of ad spend and sixty dollars of confirmed revenue. Work out the R O A S. Then, as an extra step, change the revenue to forty dollars and then thirty dollars, and see where break-even sits. Use the calculator on screen. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: ROI and ROAS are different numbers
steps.p: Beginners mix these two up and make bad calls. A ROAS of 150% is a 50% ROI. An ROI of 150% would be a ROAS of 250%. Always say which one you mean, and write its formula at the top of your sheet.
steps.say: Beginners mix these two up and make bad calls, so compare the columns. R O A S is revenue divided by spend, with break-even at one point oh. R O I is profit divided by spend, with break-even at zero percent. So a R O A S of one hundred and fifty percent is a fifty percent R O I. And an R O I of one hundred and fifty percent would be a R O A S of two hundred and fifty percent. Always say which one you mean.

steps.p: Use this to translate. ROI equals ROAS minus one, times 100. So a ROAS of 2.0 is a 100% ROI, and a ROAS of 0.8 is a 20% loss. The rule holds only when ad spend is your only cost.
steps.say: Use this table to translate. R O I equals R O A S minus one, times one hundred. So a R O A S of zero point five is minus fifty percent, you lost half the spend. One point oh is zero percent, break-even. One point five is fifty percent. And two point oh is a one hundred percent R O I, you doubled the money. One catch: this rule only holds when ad spend is your only cost.

steps.p: Ad spend is rarely your only cost. Tools, creatives, page hosting and payment fees come out of the same profit. Example: add $6 of tools and creative costs. Profit becomes $60 − $46 = $14, and ROI on total cost is $14 ÷ $46, about 30%.

d.text: Example: ROI on ad spend alone 50%. ROI after all costs about 30%.

steps.say: And ad spend is rarely your only cost. Tools, creatives, page hosting and payment fees come out of the same profit. Example: add six dollars of tools and creative costs. Profit becomes sixty minus forty six, which is fourteen dollars, and R O I on total cost is about thirty percent. So R O I on ad spend alone was fifty percent, but after all costs it's about thirty.

steps.p: Example: three ad sets each spent $40. Ad set A earned $60, B earned $40 and C earned $90. By ROI: C made 125%, A made 50% and B made 0%. C is the best candidate for budget, but only the scale rule decides when.
steps.more: Check C: ($90 − $40) ÷ $40 × 100 = 125%. With only a few conversions behind each ad set, these rankings can flip in a day. The starting scale rule asks for CPA at or below 0.8 × target with at least 3 network-confirmed conversions, and then only +20% at most every 48 hours. Full detail: Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: Look at the bars. Example: three ad sets each spent forty dollars. Ad set A earned sixty, B earned forty, and C earned ninety. By R O I, C made one hundred and twenty five percent, A made fifty, and B made zero. C is the best candidate for budget, but only the scale rule decides when. With only a few conversions behind each one, these rankings can flip in a day.

steps.p: On RevShare deals you earn a share of what the brand makes from your users over months. Day-one ROAS then looks worse than the final return. Record revenue against the day you bought the traffic, and update it as earnings come in.
steps.more: In this Example, the RevShare traffic passes break-even (ROAS 1.0) in month 4 and passes the CPA deal in month 6. Real curves differ widely. RevShare terms also differ by network: some carry negative balances forward, some pay on net revenue after costs. Read the terms. Trading and gambling RevShare is regulated activity; follow local law and platform rules.
steps.say: On RevShare deals, you earn a share of what the brand makes from your users over months. So day-one R O A S looks worse than the final return. Look at the two lines. In this Example, the RevShare line passes break-even in month four and passes the C P A deal in month six. Real curves differ widely, and terms differ by network, so read them. Record revenue against the day you bought the traffic, and update it as earnings come in. Trading and gambling RevShare is regulated, so follow local law and platform rules.

steps.p: Ask these four questions about every campaign at the end of each day. They take two minutes and stop you from funding losing campaigns just because they look busy.
d: What is ROI after all costs?
steps.say: Ask these four questions about every campaign at the end of each day. What did I spend? What did the network confirm? What's the R O I after all costs? And is E P C above C P C? They take two minutes, and they stop you funding losing campaigns just because they look busy.

steps.h: Common profit mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: These are the mistakes that make a losing campaign look fine, or a good one look bad. Each fix is a habit for your sheet.
d: Mixing up ROI and ROAS|write both formulas on the sheet
Ignoring non-ad costs|add tools and creatives
Trusting the network EPC|measure your own
Judging RevShare on day one|update revenue as it arrives
Ranking on 1 or 2 conversions|wait for the rule thresholds
steps.say: These are the mistakes that make a losing campaign look fine, or a good one look bad. Mixing up R O I and R O A S, so write both formulas on the sheet. Ignoring non-ad costs, so add tools and creatives. Trusting the network E P C, when you should measure your own. Judging RevShare on day one, instead of updating revenue as it arrives. And ranking on one or two conversions, instead of waiting for the rule thresholds.

quiz.q: You spent $50 and earned $80 in revenue. What is the ROI?
quiz.why: ROI = ($80 − $50) ÷ $50 × 100 = 60%. 160% and 1.6 are the ROAS written two ways.

quiz.q: You spent $50 and earned $80 in revenue. What is the ROAS?
quiz.why: ROAS = $80 ÷ $50 = 1.6. 0.6 is the ROI as a decimal, and 62.5% divides spend by revenue.

quiz.q: Revenue was $45 from 300 clicks. What is the EPC?
quiz.why: EPC = $45 ÷ 300 = $0.15. $6.67 comes from dividing clicks by revenue.

quiz.q: A campaign shows a ROAS of 0.9. What does that mean?
options: You lost about 10% of your spend
quiz.why: ROAS 0.9 means $0.90 came back per $1 spent, an ROI of −10%. Break-even is ROAS 1.0.

quiz.q: Your EPC is $0.12 and your CPC is $0.18. What is happening?
options: Each click earns more than it costs
EPC must always be higher, so the data is wrong
Each click costs more than it earns, so you are losing money
quiz.why: You pay $0.18 per click and earn $0.12 per click, a $0.06 loss on every click. EPC below CPC is common and means the campaign is losing.

steps.h: Know your line before you cross it
steps.p: Break-even is the point where revenue equals cost: no profit and no loss. Every metric has a break-even value. If you know them before you launch, you can tell within hours which side of the line a campaign is on, long before the month ends.

d.s: Above it you earn. Below it you pay.

steps.say: Break-even is the point where revenue equals cost: no profit, and no loss. Here's the key idea. Every metric has a break-even value. If you know them before you launch, you can tell within hours which side of the line a campaign is on, long before the month ends. Above the line, you earn. Below it, you pay.

steps.p: Every break-even number comes from your payout and your rates. Example: payout $30, lead-to-FTD rate 5.56% (2 of 36), EPC $0.25 and CTR 1.5%. Pay more than these and the campaign loses money, as long as the rates hold.
steps.more: Check the CPL line: 36 leads at $1.67 each cost $60, exactly the revenue from 2 FTDs at $30. Check the CPM line: at a $3.75 CPM, 16,000 impressions cost $60, again equal to revenue. The Example campaign paid $1.11 per lead and a $2.50 CPM, both under break-even, which is why it made a profit.
steps.say: Every break-even number comes from your payout and your rates. Look at the table. Example: payout thirty dollars, lead-to-F T D rate five point five six percent, E P C twenty five cents, and C T R one point five percent. Break-even C P A equals the payout, thirty dollars. Break-even C P L, cost per lead, is one dollar sixty seven. Break-even C P C equals E P C, twenty five cents. And break-even C P M is three dollars seventy five. Pay more than these, and the campaign loses money, as long as the rates hold.

steps.p: Example: if 5.56% of leads deposit and each FTD pays $30, each lead is worth $30 × 0.0556 = $1.67. You can pay up to $1.67 per lead and still break even. The campaign paid $1.11 per lead, which leaves room for profit.
steps.say: Let's work out break-even C P L. Example: if five point five six percent of leads deposit, and each F T D pays thirty dollars, then each lead is worth thirty dollars times that rate, which is one dollar sixty seven. You can pay up to one dollar sixty seven per lead and still break even. Our campaign paid one dollar eleven per lead, which leaves room for profit.

steps.p: An offer pays $50 per FTD and about 4% of your leads deposit. Work out the break-even CPL, the most you can pay per lead with zero profit. Set the margin to 0 for break-even, then check your answer.
steps.more: $50 × 4% = $2.00. At $2.00 per lead, 25 leads cost $50 and bring 1 FTD worth $50. Now set the margin to 25% and see the target CPL fall to $1.50.

d.task: Payout $50, 4% of leads deposit, 0% margin. What is the break-even CPL?

steps.say: Your turn. An offer pays fifty dollars per F T D, and about four percent of your leads deposit. Work out the break-even C P L, the most you can pay per lead with zero profit. Set the margin to zero for break-even in the calculator on screen. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Afterwards, try setting the margin to twenty five percent and watch the target change.

steps.p: Break-even CPL assumes the lead-to-FTD rate holds. If deposits fall from 5.56% to 3% of leads, break-even CPL drops to $30 × 0.03 = $0.90. The $1.11 per lead that used to make money now loses money. Recheck break-even every week.

d.text: When a rate changes, recalculate every break-even value that uses it.

steps.say: Here's a warning. Break-even C P L assumes the lead-to-F T D rate holds. If deposits fall from five point five six percent to three percent of leads, break-even C P L drops to thirty dollars times three percent, which is ninety cents. The one dollar eleven per lead that used to make money now loses money. So when a rate changes, recalculate every break-even value that uses it, and recheck break-even every week.

steps.p: LTV means lifetime value: the total money one customer brings you over the whole time they stay. On a CPA deal you are paid once, so LTV is the payout. On RevShare, or with your own products, value keeps arriving for months, and LTV is what you compare with cost.

d.s: Count every month a customer stays

steps.say: L T V means lifetime value, the total money one customer brings you over the whole time they stay. On a C P A deal, you're paid once, so L T V is simply the payout. But on RevShare, or with your own products, value keeps arriving for months. Then L T V is what you compare with your cost. Count every month a customer stays.

steps.p: Example: on a 30% RevShare deal, one depositing user produces $40 of net revenue for the brand in month 1, $20 in month 2 and $10 in month 3. Your share is $12, $6 and $3. Three-month LTV: $21.
steps.more: Compare this with a $30 CPA deal for the same user: over three months the CPA deal pays more, and pays sooner. RevShare comes out ahead only if users stay active long enough. Many networks also carry negative balances forward or deduct costs before your share. Read the terms, and never assume LTV from someone else's screenshot. Measure your own users over time.
steps.say: Here's an Example on a thirty percent RevShare deal. One depositing user makes forty dollars of net revenue for the brand in month one, twenty in month two, and ten in month three. Your share is twelve, six and three dollars. So the three-month L T V is twenty one dollars. Compare that with a thirty dollar C P A deal, which pays more and sooner. Many networks also carry negative balances forward, so read the terms, and never assume L T V from someone else's screenshot.

steps.p: Example: the same user under two deals. The CPA line is flat at $30 from the start. The RevShare line grows each month but, in this Example, flattens before it reaches $30. With better retention it could pass the CPA line. Your own data decides.
steps.say: Look at the two lines. Example: the same user under two deals. The C P A line is flat at thirty dollars from the start. The RevShare line grows each month but, in this Example, flattens before it reaches thirty. With better retention, it could pass the C P A line. Your own data decides which deal is better for your traffic.

steps.h: Payback: when the money comes home
steps.p: Payback is how long it takes to earn back what you spent. Example: you paid $20 per FTD. On the RevShare example, earnings reach $18 after month 2 and $21 after month 3, so you get your $20 back during month 3. Until then, that money is tied up.
steps.more: CPA deals have a payback delay too. Networks often hold new affiliates' earnings and pay on a schedule such as weekly or monthly, and terms vary by network. Your ad platform usually bills you much sooner. Plan your cash so a slow payout week does not force you to stop a campaign that is working.

d.label: months to earn back $20 per FTD

steps.say: Payback is how long it takes to earn back what you spent. Example: you paid twenty dollars per F T D. On the RevShare example, earnings reach eighteen dollars after month two and twenty one after month three. So you get your twenty dollars back during month three. Until then, that money is tied up. C P A deals have a delay too, because networks pay on a schedule while ad platforms bill sooner. So plan your cash.

steps.h: End to end: a losing day
steps.p: Example, a new campaign: $60 spent at a $3.00 CPM bought 20,000 impressions. A 1.2% CTR gave 240 clicks. 12.5% of clicks signed up, giving 30 leads. 1 lead deposited. The payout is $30. Let us read it from top to bottom.
steps.say: Now let's read a full campaign, a losing day. Example: sixty dollars spent at a three dollar C P M bought twenty thousand impressions. A one point two percent C T R gave two hundred and forty clicks. Twelve and a half percent of clicks signed up, giving thirty leads. And one lead deposited. The payout is thirty dollars. Follow the funnel from top to bottom with me.

steps.p: Example: CPC is $60 ÷ 240 = $0.25. CPL is $60 ÷ 30 = $2.00. Cost per FTD is $60. Revenue is $30, so profit is −$30, ROI is −50% and ROAS is 0.5. Every cost sits at double its break-even value.
steps.more: Break-even CPC is EPC: $30 ÷ 240 = $0.125. Break-even CPL is $30 × (1 ÷ 30) = $1.00. What do the starting rules say? With a $21 target, the zero-FTD line is $42, but this ad set has 1 FTD. CPA is judged from $63 of spend, and it has spent $60, so it is a hold for now. The kill line is the lower of $31.50 and the $30 break-even, so $30. If the next $3 brings nothing, CPA is $63 and the rules say kill. Use the time: compared with the profitable Example, the click costs more ($0.25 against $0.17) and fewer clicks sign up (12.5% against 15%). Test a new creative as a new ad set and check the page.
steps.say: Here are the numbers, next to break-even. C P C is twenty five cents, against a break-even of twelve and a half cents. C P L is two dollars, against one dollar. Cost per F T D is sixty dollars, against thirty. R O I is minus fifty percent, and R O A S is zero point five. Every cost sits at double its break-even. The rules say hold for now, because spend hasn't reached sixty three dollars yet. Use that time to test a new creative as a new ad set, and check the page.

steps.p: To get a weekly CTR, add up the clicks and the impressions, then divide. Averaging the daily CTRs gives the wrong answer when days differ in size. The same rule applies to CR, CPA, ROI and every other rate in this module.
steps.say: Here's a rule that saves a lot of confusion: never average percentages. Compare the two columns. Averaging two daily C T Rs, two percent and one percent, gives one point five. But day two was nine times bigger. Add up the clicks, one hundred and ten, and the impressions, ten thousand, and divide. The real C T R is one point one percent. The same rule applies to C R, C P A, R O I and every other rate.

steps.h: Common break-even mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: Break-even is only as good as the rates behind it. These mistakes all come from treating it as fixed. Each fix takes a minute a week.
d: Using an old deposit rate|recheck break-even weekly
Setting target equal to payout|leave a margin
Treating RevShare LTV as certain|measure your own users
Forgetting payout delays|plan cash for payback
Copying LTV from screenshots|use your own data
steps.say: Finally, the common break-even mistakes. Using an old deposit rate, so recheck break-even weekly. Setting the target equal to the payout, when you should leave a margin. Treating RevShare L T V as certain, instead of measuring your own users. Forgetting payout delays, so plan cash for payback. And copying L T V from screenshots, instead of using your own data. Each fix takes about a minute a week.

takeaways: Break-even CPA = payout, CPL = payout × lead-to-FTD rate, CPC = EPC, CPM = EPC × CTR × 1,000.
LTV is total value over time. Compare it with cost, and plan cash for payback and payout delays.
Recalculate break-even whenever a rate moves, and never average percentages.

steps.h: A sheet turns numbers into decisions
steps.p: Every number in this module is only useful if it leads to a decision: stop, wait or add money. A daily sheet does that. Without one, beginners keep losing ad sets for weeks and starve the ones that work, and both mistakes cost real money.
steps.more: The ad platform shows you numbers, but not your payout, your break-even or the network's confirmed count. Your sheet joins all three. Ten minutes a day on a sheet saves more money than any trick in an ad account, because it stops you from deciding on mood.

d.s: Ten minutes a day, same time every day

steps.say: Every number in this module is only useful if it leads to a decision: stop, wait, or add money. A daily sheet does that. Raw counts go in, decisions come out. Without one, beginners keep losing ad sets running for weeks and starve the ones that work, and both mistakes cost real money. Your sheet joins three things the ad platform won't show you together: your payout, your break-even, and the network's confirmed count.

steps.p: Use one row per ad set per day. Type in raw counts only (spend, impressions, clicks, leads, FTDs and revenue) and let formulas work out every rate. Typing rates in by hand is how mistakes get into a sheet.
steps.more: Spreadsheet formulas for row 2, where B is spend, C impressions, D clicks, E leads, F FTDs and G revenue: CPM =B2/C2*1000, CTR =D2/C2, CPC =B2/D2, CPL =B2/E2, CPA =B2/F2, Profit =G2-B2, ROI =(G2-B2)/B2, ROAS =G2/B2. Format CTR and ROI as percentages. Wrap each division in IFERROR so a day with zero FTDs shows a blank instead of an error, for example =IFERROR(B2/F2,"").

steps.h: Before you kill: check the data is real
steps.p: A zero can mean the ad set failed, or that tracking broke or deposits are late. Before acting on a kill line, confirm a test conversion appears in the network, and that the spend has had time to convert. Never send invented events to make numbers move.
steps.more: If your network reports FTDs hours after the click, judge only spend that has had time to convert. Rules when data is thin or late are in the Budget and kill rules module. Full tracking setup: Tracking setup lab module.

quiz.q: Target $21. An ad set has spent $57 with 3 confirmed FTDs. What is the call?
options: Scale +20%, because CPA $19 is below target
quiz.why: CPA is $57 ÷ 3 = $19. That is under target but above the $16.80 scale line, so the rule card says hold, not scale.

quiz.q: Your sheet shows 0 FTDs on $48 spend with a $21 target. What should you check before you kill it?
options: That tracking works and the spend has had time to convert
Whether a friend got better results
quiz.why: $48 is past the $42 line, but a zero can come from broken tracking or late deposits. Confirm a test conversion and matured spend, then apply the rule.

lessons.say_intro: This final lesson turns every number in the module into decisions. You'll build a daily tracking sheet, turn your target C P A into kill, hold and scale lines in dollars, and set up a calm daily and weekly routine.
lessons.say_outro: So, raw counts go in, formulas do the maths, and a rule card in dollars turns each row into kill, hold or scale. Your task: build your sheet with a plan tab, a daily tab and a summary tab, write your offer's rule card in dollars, then enter the four example ad sets from the worked example, and check your sheet gives the same verdicts. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You spent $60 with 0 FTDs. Your target CPA is $25. You have 300 clicks and 40 leads. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Double the budget to get data faster
Pause or change it: spend is 2.4 times the target CPA with no FTD, after checking for delayed deposits and broken tracking
Keep it running unchanged for a month
Ask the network to lower the payout
exam.why: $60 ÷ $25 = 2.4 target CPAs spent with nothing to show. Check that tracking works and that deposits are not just delayed, then pause or change something.

exam.q: Payout $30, target $21. On the day 4 check, an ad set has spent $66 with 3 confirmed FTDs. What do the starting rules say?
options: Hold, because CPA is under break-even
Kill: spend is past $63 and CPA $22 is above target
Hold: CPA $22 is above target but under the $30 kill line, and above the $16.80 scale line
exam.why: CPA is $66 ÷ 3 = $22. From $63 the kill line is the lower of $31.50 and $30, so $30. $22 is under it, so no kill, and above $16.80, so no scale. Hold.

exam.q: An ad set spent $80, got 400 clicks and earned $100 in revenue. What are its EPC, CPC and ROI?
Revenue is $110 on $50 of spend. Your partner says ROAS is 120%. You say ROI is 120%. Who is right?
options: Only you: ROI is 120% and ROAS is 220%

exam.q: The payout is $40, 5% of leads deposit and you are paying $2.60 per lead. What should you conclude?
options: It is profitable, because $2.60 is a low CPL
You need the CTR before you can decide
You lose about $0.60 per lead at these rates; cut CPL or lift lead quality
exam.why: Break-even CPL = $40 × 0.05 = $2.00. Paying $2.60 loses $0.60 per lead while the deposit rate stays at 5%.

exam.q: After 10 days, frequency is 4.2, CTR has fallen from 1.8% to 0.7% and CPM is steady. What is the best action?
options: Refresh the creative or widen the audience
exam.why: High frequency with a falling CTR at a steady CPM points to ad fatigue. New creative or a wider audience addresses it; narrowing makes fatigue worse.

exam.q: Ads Manager reports 6 purchases on $90 of spend. The network confirms 3 FTDs. Target $21, payout $30. Which decision do the starting rules support?
options: Kill: using the network count, CPA is $30 after more than $63 spend, which equals the kill line
Hold: using the network count, CPA is $30 after $90 spend, which is not above the $30 kill line
Kill, because the two counts disagree
exam.why: Use the network count: $90 ÷ 3 = $30. The kill line is $30 and the rule kills only when CPA is above it, so this is a hold, and close to a kill. The platform's $15 would wrongly suggest scaling.

exam.q: You have 1,200 link clicks and 780 landing page views, with a 20% lead rate from page views. If a faster page lifts views to 1,080 at the same rate, how many extra leads do you get?
exam.why: Before: 780 × 0.20 = 156 leads. After: 1,080 × 0.20 = 216 leads. The difference is 60 extra leads for the same spend.

exam.q: A CPA deal pays $35 now. On RevShare you estimate $10, $8, $6, $5 and $4 per FTD over five months. Your cash is tight. Which deal fits better?
options: CPA: it pays more over this period and pays sooner, which matters when cash is tight
exam.why: The RevShare estimate adds up to $33 over five months, less than $35, and it arrives slowly. With tight cash, faster payback matters too.

exam.q: Weekly totals: ad set A spent $200 and earned $260. Ad set B spent $50 and earned $90. Which has the higher ROI, and what is the combined ROI?
exam.why: A: $60 ÷ $200 = 30%. B: $40 ÷ $50 = 80%. Combined: ($350 − $250) ÷ $250 = 40%. 55% is the average of the two rates, which is wrong.
